title: Drishyam 3 Crosses ₹141 Crore Worldwide in Four Days, Cementing Mohanlal's Box-Office Reign
excerpt: The Malayalam thriller's staggering overseas haul — nearly ₹78 crore from diaspora markets — underscores how deeply the franchise resonates beyond India's borders
body:
## The Numbers That Shook an Industry

When Mohanlal's *Drishyam 3* opened on May 22, few doubted it would perform well. The franchise — centred on Georgekutty, a cable-TV operator whose quiet cunning conceals a family's darkest secret — has become the most commercially reliable property in Malayalam cinema. But the speed and scale of its box-office assault have surpassed even the most bullish projections.

In just four days, the Jeethu Joseph-directed thriller has amassed ₹141.34 crore worldwide, making it the fastest Malayalam film to breach the ₹100-crore barrier in 2026 and only the fifth Mohanlal film to enter that exclusive club.

## A Day-by-Day Reckoning

The opening day set the tone: approximately ₹43–48 crore worldwide, with ₹15.85 crore from India's net collections and an extraordinary ₹25–30 crore pouring in from overseas territories. Day two pushed the cumulative tally to roughly ₹76 crore. By the end of day three — just 58 hours after its first screening — *Drishyam 3* had crossed the ₹100-crore mark, settling at approximately ₹117 crore worldwide.

The fourth day brought the total to ₹141.34 crore: ₹63.34 crore from India's gross collections and a remarkable ₹78 crore from international markets. To put that in perspective, the overseas gross now exceeds the domestic one — a phenomenon almost unheard of for a regional-language Indian film.

## Why the Sequel Works Commercially, If Not Critically

Critical reception has been decidedly mixed. Several reviewers have noted that the narrative tension which made the original *Drishyam* a modern classic feels diluted in this third instalment. The screenplay's puzzle-box mechanics, once novel, now risk feeling formulaic. Yet audiences appear undeterred.

The franchise's commercial resilience owes much to Mohanlal's enduring stardom and the sheer gravitational pull of the Georgekutty character, who has become a folk hero — the ordinary man who outwits the powerful. Jeethu Joseph, who has directed all three instalments, understands that audiences return not for plot novelty but for the satisfaction of watching an underdog triumph through intellect rather than muscle.

A Hindi-language version featuring Ajay Devgn is being developed separately, which could extend the franchise's commercial footprint into Bollywood's far larger market.

## The Diaspora Factor: When Overseas Outpaces Home

The most striking story in *Drishyam 3*'s box-office performance is not what happened inside India but what happened outside it. The ₹78 crore overseas haul — equivalent to roughly $9 million — represents a staggering concentration of diaspora spending.

The Middle East alone accounted for approximately ₹36 crore by day three. In the UAE, 198,000 tickets were sold; across the broader Gulf region, that figure reached 345,000. These are not marginal numbers. They reflect the deep roots of the Malayali diaspora in the Gulf states, where generations of Keralite workers have maintained intense cultural connections to their home cinema.

For Non-Resident Indians, *Drishyam* is more than entertainment — it is a shared cultural reference point. The original 2013 film became a communal experience in diaspora households, discussed at family gatherings and forwarded in WhatsApp groups long before it was remade in Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu. Each sequel reactivates that community memory.

North American markets, too, have contributed significantly, with premium-format screenings in cities with substantial Indian populations — Toronto, the San Francisco Bay Area, the New York tri-state region — selling out within hours of ticket availability.

## A Shifting Industry Landscape

The overseas-heavy performance of *Drishyam 3* fits a broader pattern. Malayalam cinema has, over the past three years, quietly built the most internationally viable regional film industry in India. Films like *Manjummel Boys*, *Aadujeevitham*, and *L2: Empuraan* have demonstrated that Malayali audiences abroad will show up in numbers that rival or exceed domestic collections.

This has implications beyond Kerala. It signals to producers and distributors that investment in diaspora-facing marketing — subtitled prints, coordinated global release dates, partnerships with international exhibitors — can yield returns that fundamentally alter a film's economics.

## What Comes Next

*Drishyam 3* is expected to maintain strong collections through the weekend, with industry trackers projecting a ₹175–200 crore worldwide finish in its first week. The Hindi remake, when it arrives, could potentially push the franchise's combined global earnings into unprecedented territory for an Indian thriller series.

For Mohanlal, now 65, the film is further confirmation of his unique position in Indian cinema: a star whose box-office power shows no sign of diminishing, sustained by a diaspora audience that treats each new release as an event rather than merely a film.
nri_angle: Drishyam 3 earned ₹78 crore overseas in four days — more than its India gross — driven by massive NRI turnout in the Gulf, Middle East, and North America. The franchise is a cultural touchstone for the Malayalam diaspora.
